answers.answer: A volume is a disk-like device exposing numbered blocks. Software reads or overwrites selected ranges without replacing a whole object. The block interface moves bytes; a filesystem adds files, directories and metadata; a database adds records, queries and transactions. Attaching exposes the device and creates none of these higher layers. Provisioning allocates the volume; attaching exposes it to a host; formatting creates a filesystem; mounting makes it accessible at a host directory-tree location. First identify the intended device and inspect for existing data or a filesystem. Format only a verified empty intended volume for file use. Mount a suitable existing filesystem on a restored volume without reformatting. Automatic formatting can overwrite filesystem structures and destroy access to valuable data.

evidence.quote: A disk-like device that exposes numbered blocks.
A filesystem organizes blocks into files, directories and metadata. A database using those files adds records, queries and transaction rules.
Provisioning allocates a volume. Attaching exposes the device to a host.
Formatting creates a filesystem. Mounting makes that filesystem accessible at a location in the host's directory tree.
Formatting it overwrites filesystem structures and can destroy access to that data.

answers.answer: Persistence can retain delivered data after a process stops or an instance lifetime ends, subject to service lifecycle and deletion policy. It does not promise undeletability or continuous access. EBS can outlive EC2, but the actual delete-on-termination setting can delete a volume when its instance terminates; inspect it. An Availability Zone is a provider location/failure boundary. EBS attaches within the same zone and replicates within it against component failures. Those copies establish neither access during a whole-zone outage nor recovery from deletion. A successful buffered write may reside only in volatile application buffers or OS caches and disappear on host crash. Persistent storage cannot retain bytes never delivered to it. Use the supported application/database durability procedure: send relevant buffers onward, wait for required completion and handle errors. Linux fsync flushes file data and relevant metadata toward durable storage and waits for device completion, but cannot flush an application-only buffer. Directory entries may require syncing the containing directory. Check scope, completion result and failure model. Success covers specified data under that model, not all disasters, subsequent deletion or a complete multi-write transaction. Transaction/recovery rules remain with the application/database.

evidence.quote: Persistent storage can retain delivered data after a process stops or an instance's running life ends.
its delete-on-termination setting can remove a volume when the instance terminates.
EBS attaches a volume to instances in the same zone and replicates volume data within that zone to protect against component failures.
Copies inside one zone do not establish access during a zone-wide outage.
An ordinary buffered write can report success while recent bytes remain only in memory.
It must send the relevant buffered data onward, wait for the required completion and handle errors.
Successful durability completion covers specified data under a specified failure model.

answers.answer: No. Multi-attach exposes one device to multiple hosts where supported; it does not coordinate filesystem caches, metadata changes or application transactions. A single-host filesystem assumes control of disk structures. Independent mounts may cache stale views and make conflicting updates, overwriting data or metadata despite successful attachment. Ordinary XFS and EXT4 are not designed for simultaneous access from multiple servers. For shared named files/directories, consider a shared file service. Coordinated shared blocks require a filesystem or application expressly designed for it; verify provider attachment support and software coordination requirements.

evidence.quote: It does not itself coordinate their filesystem caches, metadata changes or application transactions.
Two independent mounts can each cache an old view and make conflicting updates, overwriting metadata or data.
If the requirement is simply shared files and directories, consider a shared file service.
Verify both provider attachment support and the software's coordination requirements; enabling a volume option does not supply those rules.

answers.answer: A snapshot preserves volume state at a point in time. EBS captures bytes written to the volume, excluding application and OS caches. Active updates may leave only some related writes stored, so snapshot success proves neither a complete transaction nor recoverability. A database may repair/replay a crash-like state; that differs from an application-consistent backup prepared at a valid application boundary. Follow the supported application/database backup procedure, coordinating flushing and pausing writes where required across all relevant volumes. Pausing alone does not flush buffers. EBS snapshot creation is asynchronous: check completion before relying on it. Restore into a volume, attach appropriately and use its existing filesystem without formatting. Retain historical points because snapshots after damaging updates can preserve damage. Test restoration and application usability, assessing acceptable data loss and recovery time.

evidence.quote: A snapshot preserves a volume's state at a point in time.
EBS snapshots capture data written to the volume, excluding bytes still in application or operating-system caches.
Snapshot success alone proves neither a complete transaction nor that the application can recover.
Coordinate flushing and pausing writes where required, including all relevant data volumes.
For EBS, snapshot creation continues asynchronously; check completion before relying on that recovery point.
Restore into a volume, attach it appropriately and use its existing filesystem without formatting.
Test restoration and application usability, including how much data and recovery time you can afford to lose.

answers.answer: Capacity measures data that fits; IOPS measures operations per second; throughput measures bytes per second; I/O latency measures time for one operation to complete. Many small random requests can hit an operation-rate limit with few bytes, whereas a large sequential scan can hit byte throughput with fewer operations. More capacity alone does not guarantee speed. Measure representative request sizes, access patterns, demand, latency and queues; excess demand increases waiting. Compare volume limits with host storage-path limits, including EBS instance bandwidth. Inspect other application bottlenecks and locate where time goes before buying more performance; a volume increase may not help a host- or application-limited workload.

evidence.quote: Capacity measures how much data fits. IOPS counts input/output operations per second. Throughput measures bytes transferred per second. I/O latency is the time one operation takes to complete.
Many small random requests can exhaust an operation-rate limit while transferring relatively few bytes.
A large sequential scan can hit a byte-throughput limit with fewer operations.
Compare both volume limits and the host's storage-path limits.
If the host or another part of the application is the bottleneck, buying more volume performance may not reduce application latency.

answers.answer: Use block storage for an OS disk or database engine updating ranges in disk-like local files because it supplies range operations. Use a shared file service for multiple hosts sharing named files/directories because it exposes shared filesystem operations. Use object storage for blobs retrieved by key. Use a database for field-queryable records and transactions because it supplies record queries and transaction behavior. A database can use files on a block volume underneath and retain responsibility for records/transactions. Operators still manage filesystem/database software, safe attachment, deletion settings, capacity, performance and tested recovery. Choose according to access patterns, sharing and recovery needs.

evidence.quote: Fits an operating-system disk or database engine updating ranges in disk-like storage.
A shared file service exposes named files, directories and filesystem operations to multiple hosts.
Provides key-based access to stored objects, useful for blobs such as media and exports.
Supplies record queries and transaction behavior.
Choosing block storage leaves filesystem or database management, safe attachment, deletion settings, capacity, performance and tested recovery to the system's operators.
